behavior.overview: This repository is a full-stack ecommerce platform implemented as a monolith. It uses Django as the backend framework to provide a REST API for core commerce features, and a React-based frontend for the user interface, state management, and interaction with the API.

partitions.name: Backend Application
partitions.role: The backend provides the API infrastructure, data modeling, and business logic for the ecommerce platform.
partitions.functionality: Manages core entities including users, products, orders, payments, reviews, and shipping addresses. It exposes REST endpoints via Django for the frontend to perform CRUD operations on these entities.

partitions.name: Frontend Application
partitions.role: The frontend serves as the interactive user interface built with React, consuming the backend API.
partitions.functionality: Handles user-facing features like product browsing, cart management, user authentication, checkout flows, and profile management, utilizing Redux for state synchronization and Axios for API communication.

partitions.name: Static Assets
partitions.role: Provides production-ready static files for the Django application.
partitions.functionality: Contains compiled CSS, JavaScript, and asset files required for the admin panel UI and the core application styling.

partitions.name: Deployment Configuration
partitions.functionality: Provides Docker configuration and environment variables required to build and deploy the Django-based monolith.

context_record.business_goal: Modernize the existing e-commerce monolith to improve scalability, maintainability, and support incremental evolution without downtime.
context_record.problem_statement: The existing monolithic architecture suffers from scalability and maintainability issues, particularly during peak traffic periods.

blueprint.selected_pattern: Strangler Fig migration from Django monolith to a selectively decomposed service architecture (event-assisted, gateway-fronted)
blueprint.rationale: The context requires higher peak-traffic capacity, high availability and incremental evolution without downtime, starting from a working Django + React system. A big-bang microservices rewrite would violate the no-downtime and incremental-evolution goals, and the repository shows a small, cohesive codebase (~1.7k LOC of Python across seven Django apps) where a service-per-app split would create far more operational cost than the requirements justify. A Strangler Fig transition places a routing seam at the edge, extracts only the capabilities with genuinely distinct scaling, data-access and change-cadence characteristics (product catalog/search/reviews, and cart), and deliberately retains the strongly transactional order-payment-inventory-shipping-identity core inside the existing Django deployment as a single consistency boundary. The pattern label names the transition itself because the design is a staged journey, not a finished end state.
blueprint.stakeholder_view: Customers browse and search the catalog, read and write product reviews, keep a shopping cart, check out and pay, and track their orders. Administrators manage products, stock, orders, shipments, refunds and review moderation. Today all of this is served by one Django deployment, so a traffic spike on catalog browsing â€” the highest-volume, lowest-value-density traffic â€” competes for the same capacity as checkout and back-office work, and every change requires redeploying everything. The modernization keeps the customer experience identical while changing how capacity is bought: the read-heavy storefront capabilities (catalog, search, reviews) and the cart are moved into separately scalable services, so promotional peaks can be absorbed where the traffic actually lands without risking the order and payment path. Order integrity, payments, inventory reservations and fulfilment stay together in one transactional core, which protects the business rule stakeholders care about most â€” no oversell, no double-charged or duplicated order. Migration is incremental and reversible: traffic for each capability is shifted gradually behind a single stable interface, so the React storefront is unaffected and any step can be rolled back without a maintenance window. Business outcome: promotional peaks are survivable, teams can release storefront changes without a full-system deployment, and modernization proceeds capability by capability rather than as one high-risk cutover.
blueprint.technical_view:
An API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer is placed in front of the existing Django deployment and becomes the single stable interface the React Storefront Frontend calls. It owns TLS termination, request routing per URL prefix, weighted/percentage traffic shifting between the legacy implementation and extracted services, JWT validation against tokens issued by Commerce Core Service, health-check-driven instance removal, and CDN/edge caching of catalog media and cacheable read responses.

The Commerce Core Service is the existing Django/DRF application, retained and hardened rather than rewritten. It keeps identity and accounts, orders, payments, inventory and reservations, shipping and fulfilment â€” capabilities that share one transactional boundary in Commerce Core Database (PostgreSQL) and must not be split across network calls if oversell and exactly-once order creation are to be preserved. It runs as a horizontally scalable stateless container set behind the gateway.

The Catalog and Search Service is the first extraction: product content, category browsing, product detail, search and product reviews. Its boundary is justified by dominant read traffic with a scaling profile independent of the transactional core, an independently evolving merchandising/content capability, and clearly separable data ownership. It owns Catalog Database (PostgreSQL) for product, category and review records and projects searchable documents into Search Index Store (OpenSearch) to satisfy typo tolerance, relevance ranking and autocomplete, which PostgreSQL full-text search does not provide cleanly. Reviews are deliberately kept inside this service rather than split out: they are read almost exclusively as part of product pages, share the product aggregate for rating rollups, and show no independent scaling, ownership or consistency driver.

The Cart Service is the second extraction, justified by a materially different data profile â€” short-lived, high-write, session-scoped state with no long-term relational integrity requirement â€” held in Cart Store (Redis) with configured persistence. It handles guest carts, cart merge on login and stock-availability checks delegated to Commerce Core Service at add-to-cart and checkout initiation.

The Event Backbone (managed message broker) carries domain events: catalog and inventory changes published by Commerce Core Service and Catalog and Search Service, and order lifecycle and shipment events published by Commerce Core Service. Notification Service consumes these to send verification, order confirmation, status-change and low-stock messages asynchronously, removing email work from the synchronous request path. Events also enable read-model projection into Search Index Store and availability flags in Catalog Database, giving eventual consistency where it is acceptable and keeping strong consistency where money and stock are involved.

Observability Platform collects request metrics, traces and logs from every component, backs the latency and availability acceptance criteria, and is established before any extraction so migration steps can be validated and reverted on evidence.

All services are packaged as containers (the repository already contains Docker/compose configuration) and deployed to a managed container platform with rolling deployments, readiness/liveness probes and horizontal autoscaling. No cloud provider is mandated by the context, so the design stays on portable, cloud-agnostic building blocks (containers, PostgreSQL, Redis, OpenSearch, a managed broker) that map onto any major provider.

assumptions: ASSUMPTION: The current Django monolith uses a relational database (PostgreSQL assumed) as its single store; the repository shows Django ORM migrations but no explicit database engine configuration was inspected.
ASSUMPTION: The repository's PayPal frontend dependencies indicate an external payment provider is already in use and remains the payment integration.

ASSUMPTION: Exact peak-traffic multiple, latency percentile targets and availability percentage are not stated in the Context Record; they must be agreed with stakeholders and then measured via Observability Platform before the target-state load test.
ASSUMPTION: A managed container platform with rolling deployment and autoscaling is available or will be provisioned; no orchestration platform exists in the repository beyond local Docker Compose.
ASSUMPTION: Guest-cart retention period, review moderation policy and low-stock thresholds are business parameters to be supplied.
ASSUMPTION: A single delivery team initially; team-ownership boundaries were therefore not used as a decomposition driver.
open_risks: Eventual consistency between Commerce Core Database inventory and the availability flags projected into Catalog Database and Search Index Store can briefly show a product as available after it sells out; checkout-time re-validation in Commerce Core Service is the mitigation but stale storefront reads remain visible.

Splitting catalog data out of the shared database removes the current ORM joins between orders/reviews and products (visible in the repository's cross-app serializer dependencies); order line items must be denormalized with product snapshots, which is a behavioural change requiring regression testing.
Operational complexity increases with a gateway, broker, search index and Redis; without sufficient platform capability this may cost more availability than it buys.
No quantitative peak-load, latency or availability target exists yet, so FEAT-011, FEAT-012 and FEAT-013 cannot be objectively accepted until targets are agreed.
Search relevance and typo tolerance quality depends on index mapping and analyzer tuning that cannot be validated from the repository alone.
Session/JWT handling currently lives inside the Django user app; moving validation to the edge risks subtle auth-behaviour differences and needs explicit contract tests.

migration_steps.title: Establish the edge seam and observability baseline
migration_steps.objective: Create the routing and measurement preconditions for every later extraction. This is first because no capability can be moved reversibly without a stable front door and no target can be validated without baseline telemetry.
changes: Introduce API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer in front of the existing Django deployment, which is renamed Commerce Core Service, with all routes initially pointing at it
Introduce Observability Platform and instrument Commerce Core Service and API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer with request metrics, traces, logs and latency percentiles
Containerize Commerce Core Service for a managed container platform with readiness/liveness probes, multiple replicas and rolling deployment
Agree and document the peak-traffic multiple, latency percentiles and availability target with stakeholders
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: No data changes. Commerce Core Database remains the single store and Commerce Core Service remains the sole implementation; the gateway is a transparent pass-through so the React Storefront Frontend is unchanged.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All storefront and admin traffic flows through API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer, baseline latency and error-rate dashboards exist in Observability Platform, and a rolling deployment of Commerce Core Service completes with no customer-visible failures.

migration_steps.title: Introduce the Event Backbone and publish domain events from Commerce Core Service
migration_steps.objective: Provide the asynchronous seam that later extractions need for read-model projection and notifications, while the monolith is still the single source of truth and events are consumed by nothing critical.
changes: Deploy Event Backbone as a managed message broker
Commerce Core Service publishes product-updated, inventory-changed, order-status-changed and shipment-created events at existing transaction boundaries
Define event schemas and a compatibility policy
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Events are additive and initially unconsumed; Commerce Core Database stays authoritative for all data. Publishing is transactional-outbox based so events cannot diverge from committed state.
migration_steps.exit_condition: Events are observably published for every relevant state change and can be replayed, with no change to synchronous behaviour.

migration_steps.title: Extract Catalog and Search Service on the read path
migration_steps.objective: Move the highest-volume, most read-dominated traffic off the transactional core first, because it delivers the largest peak-capacity benefit at the lowest transactional risk.
changes: Deploy Catalog and Search Service serving catalog browsing, product detail, search, autocomplete and review reads
Deploy Search Index Store and populate it from Event Backbone product-updated and inventory-changed events
Deploy Catalog Database as a read projection of product, category and review data
Configure weighted traffic shifting in API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer for catalog, search and review read routes
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Commerce Core Database remains the write source of truth; Catalog Database and Search Index Store are event-fed projections. Read traffic is shifted in increments and can be reverted to Commerce Core Service at the gateway within minutes. Writes still go to Commerce Core Service.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All catalog, search and review read traffic is served by Catalog and Search Service, response comparison against Commerce Core Service shows no functional regression, and latency at peak is within the agreed target in Observability Platform.

migration_steps.title: Transfer catalog and review data ownership to Catalog and Search Service
migration_steps.objective: Complete the bounded context so the service can evolve and deploy independently rather than remaining a read cache of the monolith.
changes: Move product, category, image and review write endpoints (including admin product editing and review moderation) to Catalog and Search Service
Catalog Database becomes the source of truth for product content and reviews; corresponding tables in Commerce Core Database are retired after cutover
Catalog and Search Service publishes product-updated and review-approved events to Event Backbone
Commerce Core Service stores product snapshots on order line items instead of relational joins to product tables
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: One-way backfill and a short dual-write window with reconciliation checks, then a route cutover at API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer. Commerce Core Service continues to own inventory quantities and publishes inventory-changed events consumed by Catalog and Search Service for availability display.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All product and review writes are handled by Catalog and Search Service, legacy catalog write paths are removed, and order creation works against product snapshots with regression tests passing.

migration_steps.title: Extract Cart Service
migration_steps.objective: Separate short-lived, high-write session state from the relational transactional core so cart traffic scales independently and no longer consumes Commerce Core Database capacity at peak.
changes: Deploy Cart Service and Cart Store handling guest carts, authenticated carts, quantity updates and cart merge on login
Cart Service calls Commerce Core Service for stock availability at add-to-cart and checkout initiation

migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Carts are transient, so existing carts are allowed to drain rather than being migrated: new carts are created in Cart Store while in-flight legacy carts continue to be served by Commerce Core Service until expiry. Checkout hand-off passes an immutable cart snapshot to Commerce Core Service, which remains authoritative for reservation and order creation.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All new cart operations are served by Cart Service, legacy cart state has drained, and cart latency at peak meets the agreed target.

changes: Deploy Notification Service consuming order-status-changed, shipment-created, account-verification-requested and low-stock events from Event Backbone
Remove synchronous email sending from Commerce Core Service request handlers
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: Run in shadow mode first (events consumed, sending suppressed) to verify message parity, then disable monolith sending and enable Notification Service delivery. Notification Service holds only delivery state, not business data.
migration_steps.exit_condition: All customer and administrator notifications are sent by Notification Service with delivery metrics visible in Observability Platform and no duplicate messages.

migration_steps.title: Consolidate and validate the target state
migration_steps.objective: Confirm the retained core is the right final boundary and prove the peak-traffic and availability goals against the agreed targets.
changes: Modularize identity, order, payment, inventory and shipping inside Commerce Core Service with explicit internal interfaces, retaining them as one transactional boundary and one deployable
Tune independent autoscaling policies per service in API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer, Catalog and Search Service, Cart Service and Commerce Core Service
Run a full peak-load test and a business-hours rolling deployment and instance-failure exercise
Document criteria that would justify any further extraction from Commerce Core Service in a later phase
migration_steps.coexistence_or_data_strategy: No further data ownership moves in this phase; Commerce Core Database keeps identity, order, payment, inventory and shipment data as the single strong-consistency boundary.
migration_steps.exit_condition: The documented peak-load test sustains the agreed traffic level within the agreed error-rate and latency thresholds, a release and an instance loss are both absorbed without customer-visible outage, and each remaining monolith capability has a stated retain-or-extract decision.

adrs.title: ADR-001: Modernize via a Strangler Fig transition behind an API gateway rather than a big-bang rewrite
adrs.context: The business goal explicitly requires incremental evolution without downtime, while the current system is a single Django deployment serving a React frontend. A full rewrite or simultaneous decomposition would require a cutover window and would put all functionality at risk at once.
adrs.decision: Introduce API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer as a stable single interface in front of the existing Django deployment (retained as Commerce Core Service), then extract capabilities one at a time with reversible, weighted traffic shifting at the gateway.
adrs.rationale: A routing seam lets each capability be moved and, if necessary, reverted without touching the React Storefront Frontend or scheduling a maintenance window. It also makes the migration measurable step by step instead of a single high-risk event, which directly serves the no-downtime and incremental-evolution requirements.
alternatives_considered: Big-bang rewrite into microservices â€” rejected: incompatible with the no-downtime requirement and disproportionate to a ~1.7k LOC Python codebase
Frontend-side routing to new services â€” rejected: forces breaking frontend changes on every migration step, violating FEAT-014
Keep the monolith unchanged and scale it vertically â€” rejected: does not separate read-heavy storefront load from transactional load and leaves the maintainability problem untouched
positive_consequences: Every migration step is independently reversible
React Storefront Frontend contract stays stable throughout
Cross-cutting concerns (TLS, auth validation, caching, health checks) are centralized
negative_consequences: The gateway becomes a critical path component requiring redundancy
Routing configuration becomes an operational artifact that must be versioned and tested
related_component_names: API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer

adrs.title: ADR-002: Extract a single Catalog and Search Service covering product content, search and reviews
adrs.context: Product browsing, search and review reads dominate customer-facing traffic and are the load that spikes during promotions, yet in the repository they share one deployment and one database with orders, payments and inventory. The repository also shows review serializers depending on product serializers, indicating tight cohesion between reviews and product content.
adrs.decision: Extract one service â€” Catalog and Search Service â€” owning product, category, image, search and review capabilities, backed by Catalog Database, rather than separate product, search and review services.
adrs.rationale: Separation from the core is justified by a distinct scaling profile (read-dominated, cacheable), separable data ownership, and an independently evolving merchandising capability. Splitting reviews or search into their own deployables is not justified: reviews are read almost exclusively as part of product pages and contribute to the product rating rollup, and search is a query surface over the same data. Grouping them keeps the smallest decomposition that meets the requirements and avoids a distributed join on the hottest read path.
alternatives_considered: Separate Product Service, Search Service and Review Service â€” rejected: no independent scaling, consistency or ownership driver, and it would split the product-page read across three network calls
Leave catalog inside the monolith and only add caching â€” rejected: does not allow storefront capacity to scale independently of the transactional core (FEAT-011)
positive_consequences: Storefront read capacity scales independently of checkout and back-office load
Product page assembly stays a local operation
Merchandising changes can be released without redeploying the transactional core
negative_consequences: Order line items must carry product snapshots instead of joining product tables
Availability data becomes eventually consistent on the storefront and must be re-validated at checkout

adrs.title: ADR-003: Introduce a dedicated search index alongside the relational catalog store
adrs.context: FEAT-004 requires typo-tolerant, relevance-ranked search with autocomplete over product name, description and attributes, and FEAT-013 requires those responses to meet latency targets at peak. The current implementation is plain Django ORM querying, with no search technology present in the repository.
adrs.decision: Add Search Index Store (OpenSearch or an equivalent managed search engine) owned by Catalog and Search Service, populated by projection from Catalog Database and inventory events, while PostgreSQL remains the system of record for catalog data.
adrs.rationale: This is a data-access pattern the existing relational store does not serve cleanly: fuzzy matching, per-field relevance weighting and prefix autocomplete are native to a search engine and awkward and slow to emulate in SQL at peak read volumes. The relational store is retained as the source of truth, so the change is additive rather than a store replacement.
alternatives_considered: PostgreSQL full-text search â€” rejected: workable for basic keyword matching but weak on typo tolerance, relevance tuning and autocomplete latency at peak
Third-party hosted search SaaS â€” viable, deferred: no budget or cloud constraint is stated to decide it; the interface is kept behind Catalog and Search Service so it stays swappable
positive_consequences: Meets the typo-tolerance, relevance and autocomplete acceptance criteria
Search load is isolated from the transactional database
negative_consequences: Introduces an index that can drift from the source of truth and needs reindexing tooling
Adds an operational component with its own capacity and cost profile

adrs.title: ADR-004: Extract Cart Service with a key-value cart store
adrs.context: In the repository the cart exists only as React Redux state (frontend/src/store/cart) with no backend persistence, yet FEAT-005 requires guest-cart persistence across browser sessions and merge into the account cart on login. Cart traffic is high-frequency, short-lived and write-heavy.
adrs.decision: Introduce Cart Service backed by Cart Store (Redis with persistence enabled) as a separate deployable, with stock validation delegated synchronously to Commerce Core Service.
adrs.rationale: Cart state has a materially different data profile from the transactional core â€” ephemeral, TTL-bounded, high write rate, no long-term referential integrity requirement â€” and a peak scaling curve that follows browsing rather than purchasing. Placing it in the relational core would add the heaviest write load to the database that must stay reliable for orders and payments. Because the capability does not exist server-side today, this is new construction rather than a technology swap.
alternatives_considered: Persist carts in Commerce Core Database â€” rejected: puts the highest-frequency write traffic on the transactional store that FEAT-006 and FEAT-008 depend on
Keep the cart entirely client-side as today â€” rejected: cannot satisfy cross-session guest persistence or server-side merge on login
positive_consequences: Cart traffic scales independently and does not contend with order processing
Low-latency cart operations supporting FEAT-013
negative_consequences: A cross-service call is needed for stock validation, adding a coupling on the add-to-cart path
Redis durability configuration must be explicit to avoid losing guest carts on failover

adrs.title: ADR-005: Retain identity, orders, payments, inventory and shipping together in Commerce Core Service
adrs.context: FEAT-006 requires exactly-once order creation and atomic stock reservation, FEAT-008 requires that concurrent checkouts never drive stock below zero, and FEAT-009 ties shipments to orders. In the repository these capabilities are already coupled through shared serializers and foreign keys across the order, payment, address, user and product apps.
adrs.decision: Keep identity/accounts, orders, payments, inventory and shipping inside a single deployable Commerce Core Service over Commerce Core Database, modularized internally with explicit interfaces but not split into separate services in this phase.
adrs.rationale: These capabilities form one transactional and consistency boundary; separating them would require distributed sagas and compensations to preserve the no-oversell and exactly-once guarantees the business depends on, buying operational complexity with no stated scaling, ownership or compliance driver to justify it. Existing Django app modules are evidence of capabilities, not of service boundaries. The peak-traffic requirement is met by relieving this core of catalog, search and cart load rather than by fragmenting it.
alternatives_considered: Service per Django app (user, order, payment, address, product, review) â€” rejected: maps modules to services with no supporting driver and forces distributed transactions across the checkout path
Separate Identity Service now â€” deferred: no independent scaling, compliance or ownership driver is stated today; criteria for revisiting are recorded in the final migration step
positive_consequences: Order, payment, reservation and refund flows stay in local ACID transactions
Materially lower operational complexity and cost during and after migration
Existing Django code is reused rather than rewritten
negative_consequences: This core remains a larger deployment unit with a shared release cadence
If one of these capabilities later develops a distinct scaling profile, a further extraction will be needed

adrs.title: ADR-006: Use an event backbone for cross-service projection and asynchronous notification
adrs.context: Once catalog data is owned by Catalog and Search Service while inventory stays in Commerce Core Service, storefront availability display needs updating without synchronous coupling. Notifications for order status, shipment and low stock must not block request handling on third-party email availability.
adrs.decision: Introduce Event Backbone as a managed message broker carrying inventory, order, shipment and catalog domain events, published via a transactional outbox and consumed by Catalog and Search Service and Notification Service.
adrs.rationale: Asynchronous events decouple the read-model projection and messaging paths from the synchronous request path, which improves fault isolation and peak throughput, and e-commerce state changes are naturally event-shaped. The outbox pattern keeps published events consistent with committed database state so projections cannot diverge silently.
alternatives_considered: Synchronous service-to-service calls for availability and email â€” rejected: couples storefront latency and checkout success to downstream availability
Periodic batch reindexing only â€” rejected: availability staleness would be measured in minutes, worsening the oversell display risk
positive_consequences: Notification and indexing failures do not fail customer requests
New consumers can be added without changing producers
Supports incremental migration by letting new services build read models before owning writes
negative_consequences: Eventual consistency on storefront availability display
Event schema evolution and replay/idempotency handling become ongoing responsibilities

adrs.title: ADR-007: Retain Python/Django and React as the default implementation technologies
adrs.context: The repository is Django + Django REST Framework on the backend and React with Redux on the frontend. Extracted services could in principle be written in another language.
adrs.decision: Implement Catalog and Search Service, Cart Service and Notification Service in Python with Django REST Framework, keep Commerce Core Service on Django, and keep React Storefront Frontend as the frontend, reusing existing models, serializers and view logic where the capability already exists.
adrs.rationale: No stated requirement is unmet by the existing stack: the peak-traffic goal is addressed by horizontal scaling and workload separation, not by language change. Reusing the existing serializers and models lowers migration risk and cost, and keeps one skill set across services. Polyglot implementation is not justified by novelty alone.
alternatives_considered: Rewrite extracted services in a different language for throughput â€” rejected: no repository-evidenced or requirement-linked performance problem attributable to Python/Django, and it would discard reusable domain logic
Replace React with another frontend framework â€” rejected: the frontend is not implicated in the scalability or maintainability problem and must remain unchanged during migration (FEAT-014)
positive_consequences: Existing domain logic and migrations are reused, shrinking extraction effort
Single toolchain, test approach and operational skill set
negative_consequences: Per-instance throughput of a Python stack means scaling is achieved with more instances, increasing infrastructure cost at peak

adrs.title: ADR-008: Establish observability and agree quantitative targets before extraction, deploying all services as stateless replicated containers
adrs.context: The Context Record states scalability, availability and responsiveness requirements only qualitatively â€” 'substantially higher peak traffic', 'high availability', 'responsive interactions' â€” with no numbers. FEAT-011, FEAT-012 and FEAT-013 all require measurable acceptance.
adrs.decision: Introduce Observability Platform as the first migration step, capture a baseline, have stakeholders agree the peak multiple, latency percentiles and availability target, and run every service as a stateless, health-checked, horizontally scalable container set with rolling deployment behind API Gateway and Edge Routing Layer.
adrs.rationale: Targets that are not stated must be agreed and measured rather than assumed; inventing figures would make the acceptance criteria unverifiable. Statelessness plus health checks and rolling releases is the mechanism that makes both independent scaling and release-without-downtime possible, and telemetry is what proves each migration step was safe and permits fast rollback.
alternatives_considered: Assume industry-standard latency and availability numbers â€” rejected: fabricated targets cannot be validated against stakeholder intent
Add observability after migration â€” rejected: removes the evidence needed to shift or revert traffic safely
positive_consequences: Each migration step is validated on evidence and reversible
Latency and availability regressions raise alerts rather than being discovered by customers
negative_consequences: Targets remain open until stakeholders agree them, so final acceptance of FEAT-011 to FEAT-013 is blocked on that input
Telemetry storage and tooling add cost

judgment_reasons.repo_grounding: The design repeatedly cites concrete repository facts: ~1.7k LOC Python across seven Django apps, cross-app serializer dependencies (review/serializers.py -> product/serializers.py; order/serializers.py -> product/user/payment serializers) used to justify keeping reviews with catalog and the transactional core together, the absence of any backend cart (cart exists only as frontend/src/store/cart Redux state) driving ADR-004's 'new construction' framing, PayPal frontend dependencies (@paypal/paypal-js, react-paypal-button-v2) identified as the existing Payment Provider, and the existing Docker/compose configuration noted as the containerization starting point. The DB engine gap is flagged as an explicit assumption rather than invented.
judgment_reasons.flaw_detection: The design targets the stated structural cause â€” one Django deployment where read-heavy catalog/search traffic contends with the transactional checkout path and every change forces a full redeploy â€” rather than renaming modules as services. Decomposition is deliberately minimal and each standalone service carries a concrete boundary rationale: Catalog and Search (read-dominated scaling profile, separable ownership, reviews kept inside because they are read as part of the product aggregate), Cart (ephemeral high-write session state, no relational integrity need), Notification (asynchronous fault isolation), while identity/order/payment/inventory/shipping are explicitly retained as one ACID boundary with service-per-Django-app rejected in ADR-005. Migration_steps are coherent and incremental: gateway seam + observability first, outbox-based events next, catalog read-path extraction with weighted shifting before ownership transfer (backfill, short dual-write, reconciliation, route cutover, product snapshots on order lines), cart carts drained rather than migrated, notifications shadow-mode first, then target-state validation â€” coexistence and reversibility are stated at every step and no big-bang cutover is hidden.
judgment_reasons.adr_soundness: ADR rationales are internally consistent and tied to locked context and repo evidence, with credible alternatives and honest negatives (gateway as critical path, index drift, eventual availability staleness, larger core deployable). Technology changes from the detected stack are each requirement-linked: OpenSearch justified by FEAT-004 typo tolerance/relevance/autocomplete which PostgreSQL FTS serves poorly (ADR-003, with SaaS alternative deferred); Redis justified by the ephemeral high-write cart profile and protecting the transactional DB (ADR-004); event broker justified by decoupling projection and email from the request path with outbox for consistency (ADR-006). ADR-007 explicitly resists novelty by retaining Python/Django and React with a stated rationale that no requirement is unmet by the existing stack.

Microservices architecture has emerged as a compelling alternative, offering the promise of enhanced scalability, improved fault tolerance, and greater development agility [1]. By decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, independently deployable services, organizations can achieve better resource utilization, faster deployment cycles, and improved system resilience.

Event-driven architecture (EDA) patterns have gained particular attention in the context of microservices migration, especially for e-commerce systems where business processes are inherently event-oriented. Customer actions such as placing orders, updating profiles, or processing payments naturally translate to domain events that can drive system behavior [5]. The asynchronous nature of event-driven communication provides better decoupling between services, enhanced fault tolerance, and improved scalability compared to synchronous request-response patterns [4].

## 2.2 Monolithic and Microservices Architectures Comparison *(printed p. 478)*

In the e-commerce landscape, choosing between microservices and traditional monolithic architectures requires careful consideration of various factors. Monolithic architectures, characterized by their single, tightly coupled codebase. However, when e-commerce systems increase in size, they frequently face scalability and maintenance issues. Microservices provide an alternative approach by decomposing monolithic applications into smaller, self-contained services [6]. This decomposition results in fine-grained services, each focusing on a specific business capability. Scalability is one of the most major advantages of microservices. E-commerce platforms often experience fluctuating traffic patterns, especially during promotions or seasonal events. Microservices enable organisations to scale individual services, ensuring that resources are deployed efficiently to manage workload properly.

## Introduction â€” relevante AbsÃ¤tze zur E-Commerce-Migration *(printed p. 2)*

The rapid evolution of e-commerce platforms has necessitated architectural paradigm shifts to meet increasing demands for scalability, reliability, and agility [2]. Traditional monolithic architectures, while providing simplicity in development and deployment, often become bottlenecks as e-commerce systems scale to handle millions of transactions and users [3]. The centralized nature of monolithic systems creates inherent limitations in terms of independent scaling, technology diversity, and fault isolation, making them unsuitable for modern e-commerce requirements.

features.name: Customer registration and authentication
features.description: Customers can create an account with email and password, verify their email, log in, log out, and reset a forgotten password. Sessions must remain valid across the customer-facing application.
features.scenario: A new visitor submits the registration form with a unique email and valid password, receives a verification email, confirms the address, and then logs in successfully and is returned to the page they started from.
acceptance_criteria: Registration with an already-registered email is rejected with a clear error message
Verification email is sent within 60 seconds of registration
Login with correct credentials establishes an authenticated session; incorrect credentials are rejected without revealing which field was wrong
Password reset link is single-use and expires
Authentication requests respond within the agreed responsive-interaction budget under normal load

features.name: User account and profile management
features.description: Authenticated customers can view and edit profile details, manage multiple shipping and billing addresses, change password, and view their order history entry points. Administrators can view and deactivate customer accounts.
features.scenario: A logged-in customer opens 'My Account', adds a second shipping address, marks it as default, changes their display name, and sees both changes reflected immediately on reload.
acceptance_criteria: Profile changes persist and are visible after re-login
A customer can store, edit and delete multiple addresses and designate one default
Password change requires the current password
An administrator can deactivate an account and the deactivated user can no longer log in
A customer can only read or modify their own account data

features.name: Product catalog browsing
features.description: Customers can browse products by category, apply filters and sorting, use pagination, and open a product detail page showing images, description, price, variants and availability.
features.scenario: A customer opens the 'Laptops' category, filters by price range and brand, sorts by price ascending, pages to result page 2, and clicks a product to see its detail page with images, price and stock status.
acceptance_criteria: Category listing returns paginated results with stable ordering
Filters and sort options can be combined and are reflected in a shareable URL
Product detail page shows title, images, description, price, variants and current availability
Catalog list pages render within the responsive-interaction target under normal load
Unavailable or unpublished products are not shown to customers

features.name: Product search
features.description: Customers can search the catalog by free-text keyword with typo tolerance, receive relevance-ranked results, refine results with the same filters as browsing, and see autocomplete suggestions.
features.scenario: A customer types 'wireles keyboad' into the search box, sees autocomplete suggestions after three characters, submits the query, and receives relevance-ranked keyboard products despite the typos.
acceptance_criteria: Keyword search returns relevance-ranked matches on product name, description and attributes
Common misspellings still return the expected products
Autocomplete suggestions appear for queries of three or more characters
A query with no matches returns an explicit empty-state with suggestions instead of an error
Search results respond within the responsive-interaction target under normal load

features.name: Shopping cart
features.description: Customers can add products (including variants) to a cart, change quantities, remove lines, and see a running subtotal. Carts persist for guests via session and merge into the account cart on login.
features.scenario: A guest adds two items to the cart, closes the browser tab, returns, sees the cart intact, then logs in and finds the guest cart merged with the three items already saved in their account cart.
acceptance_criteria: Adding, updating quantity and removing a line updates the subtotal immediately
Guest cart persists across browser sessions for a defined retention period
Guest cart merges into the account cart on login without duplicating identical lines
Quantity requested above available stock is rejected or capped with a clear message
Cart operations respond within the responsive-interaction target under normal load

features.name: Checkout and payment processing
features.description: Customers complete a checkout flow covering shipping address, shipping method, payment, and order review, with payment authorized through a payment provider. Failed payments do not create confirmed orders and stock is reserved only on successful authorization.
features.scenario: A customer proceeds to checkout, selects a saved address and a shipping method, enters card details, and receives an order confirmation page and email after successful payment authorization.
acceptance_criteria: Order totals include item subtotal, shipping cost and taxes and match the amount charged
A declined payment leaves no confirmed order and returns the customer to payment entry with a clear message
A successfully paid order is created exactly once even if the confirmation request is retried or resubmitted
Stock is decremented or reserved atomically at order confirmation so oversell does not occur
Order confirmation email is sent after successful payment
Card data is never persisted by the system

features.name: Order management and tracking
features.description: Customers can view their order history, order details and current status, and cancel eligible orders. Administrators can list, search and update orders and process refunds or cancellations.
features.scenario: A customer opens 'My Orders', selects a recent order, sees status 'Shipped' with a tracking number and per-item detail, while an administrator searching by order number updates a different order to 'Cancelled' and issues a refund.
acceptance_criteria: Customers see only their own orders, listed newest first
Order detail shows line items, totals, payment status, shipping address and current fulfilment status
Status transitions follow a defined lifecycle and invalid transitions are rejected
Customers receive a notification when order status changes
Administrators can search orders by order number, customer email and status, and record a refund or cancellation with an audit trail

features.name: Inventory management
features.description: Administrators can maintain stock levels per product variant, view current and reserved quantities, and receive low-stock alerts. Stock is reserved at checkout, decremented at fulfilment, and released when an order is cancelled or a reservation expires.
features.scenario: An administrator sets stock for a variant to 5; five customers check out concurrently and all succeed, a sixth is told the item is out of stock, and when one order is cancelled the stock returns to 1 available.
acceptance_criteria: Administrators can view and adjust stock per variant with each adjustment recorded with actor and timestamp
Concurrent checkouts never reduce available stock below zero
Cancelled orders and expired reservations return stock to available
Products with zero available stock are shown as out of stock in catalog and search
Low-stock threshold breaches raise an alert to administrators

features.name: Shipping and fulfilment
features.description: The system offers shipping options with calculated costs and delivery estimates at checkout, allows administrators to create shipments and record carrier tracking numbers, and exposes tracking information to customers.
features.scenario: An administrator marks a paid order as packed, creates a shipment with carrier and tracking number, and the customer immediately sees status 'Shipped' with a working tracking link in their order detail page.
acceptance_criteria: Available shipping methods with cost and delivery estimate are shown at checkout based on destination
Administrators can create one or more shipments per order, including partial shipments
Recording a tracking number updates the order status and notifies the customer
Customers can see carrier and tracking reference on the order detail page
Shipping cost applied at checkout equals the cost recorded on the order

features.name: Product reviews and ratings
features.description: Authenticated customers can submit a star rating and written review for products, edit or delete their own review, and see aggregate ratings on catalog and product pages. Administrators can moderate reviews.
features.scenario: A customer who purchased a product submits a 4-star review with text; after moderation approval it appears on the product page and the product's average rating and review count update accordingly.
acceptance_criteria: Only authenticated customers can submit reviews, and at most one review per customer per product
A review captures a 1-5 star rating and optional text
Average rating and review count are displayed on the product detail page and update after a review is approved, edited or deleted
A customer can edit or delete only their own review
Administrators can approve, reject or remove reviews and rejected reviews are not publicly visible

features.name: Peak-traffic scalability and elastic capacity
features.description: The platform must sustain substantially higher peak traffic than the current monolith, scaling read-heavy customer-facing capabilities independently of administrative and back-office functions without service degradation.
features.scenario: During a simulated flash-sale load test, traffic rises to the agreed peak multiple of current baseline over ten minutes; catalog, search, cart and checkout continue to serve requests within their latency targets and the error rate stays below the agreed threshold.
acceptance_criteria: A documented load test demonstrates the target peak request rate is sustained for the agreed duration
Error rate stays below the agreed threshold throughout the peak load test
Capacity for high-traffic customer-facing capabilities can be increased without redeploying or scaling unrelated capabilities
Throughput degrades gracefully rather than failing outright when the peak target is exceeded

features.name: High availability and zero-downtime evolution
features.description: The platform stays available during peak periods and during releases, with redundancy for critical customer-facing paths, health checks, and incremental rollout so functionality can be migrated off the monolith without downtime.
features.scenario: A new version of the checkout capability is deployed during business hours while live traffic is flowing; monitoring shows no failed customer requests and no maintenance window is required, and a subsequent instance failure is absorbed with requests served by remaining instances.
acceptance_criteria: Deployments complete with zero failed customer requests attributable to the release
Loss of a single instance of any critical customer-facing capability does not cause a customer-visible outage
Health checks automatically remove unhealthy instances from serving traffic
A failed release can be rolled back without data loss and within the agreed recovery time
Availability of customer-facing endpoints meets the agreed target measured over peak periods

features.name: Responsive customer-facing interactions
features.description: Customer-facing interactions such as browsing, search, cart updates and checkout steps must meet defined latency targets at peak load, with observability in place to measure and alert on regressions.
features.scenario: Under peak load, the 95th-percentile response time for catalog listing, search, add-to-cart and checkout step transitions is measured from production telemetry and each stays within its documented target.
acceptance_criteria: Latency targets are documented per customer-facing interaction
95th-percentile latency for each targeted interaction is met at peak load
Response-time metrics are captured continuously and visible in a dashboard
An alert fires when an interaction breaches its latency target for a sustained period

features.name: Incremental migration coexistence with existing systems
features.description: Capabilities can be migrated out of the Django monolith one at a time while the React frontend continues to work against a consistent interface, allowing old and new implementations to coexist and traffic to be shifted gradually and reversibly.
features.scenario: The product search capability is moved out of the monolith; traffic is shifted from the monolith implementation to the new one in stages, the React frontend is unchanged, and the shift is reversed within minutes when an anomaly is detected.
acceptance_criteria: The React frontend requires no breaking change when a capability is migrated
Traffic for a migrated capability can be shifted incrementally and reverted without downtime
Migrated and not-yet-migrated capabilities operate consistently against shared data during the transition
Each migration step is validated by regression tests covering the affected customer journeys
